eras.name: Roma
eras.note: A young republic: the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, was traditionally expelled in 509 BC. Rome dominates Latium and has just signed its first treaty with Carthage (Polybius 3.22).

eras.name: Roma
eras.note: Capital of the empire and the largest city in the world, with perhaps a million inhabitants, fed by grain fleets from Egypt, Africa and Sicily.

eras.name: Roma
eras.note: Still the symbolic capital, ringed by the new Aurelian Walls (270s), with the vast Baths of Diocletian (298–306) going up. But the emperors now rarely visit, ruling from frontier capitals.

eras.name: Roma
eras.note: Still the seat of the Senate and the Pope, but ruled by the Ostrogothic king Theoderic, who visited the city in 500. Its population has fallen dramatically since the sacks of 410 and 455.

eras.name: Roma
eras.note: Recovered by Justinian after the ruinous Gothic War (535–554), when it changed hands several times. Its population has collapsed and the aqueducts are broken.

eras.name: Caere (Cisra)
eras.note: Wealthy Etruscan city. At its port of Pyrgi the gold "Pyrgi tablets" (c. 500 BC), in Etruscan and Phoenician, record King Thefarie Velianas honouring Uni-Astarte — evidence of the Etruscan–Carthaginian alliance.

eras.name: Kyme (Cumae)
eras.note: The oldest Greek colony on the Italian mainland. Under the tyrant Aristodemus it fought off the Etruscans and sold grain to Rome during the famine of 492 BC (Livy 2.34).

eras.name: Ostia
eras.note: Rome's river-mouth port, where cargo was transferred to barges for the trip up the Tiber.

eras.name: Portus & Ostia
eras.note: Trajan's hexagonal harbour at Portus has taken over most of Ostia's trade.

eras.name: Portus Romae
eras.note: The artificial harbour built by Claudius and Trajan beside Ostia, still Rome's gateway to the sea.

eras.name: Portus
eras.note: Rome's harbour, fought over in the Gothic War.

eras.name: Puteoli
eras.note: The great port of Campania and main arrival point of the Alexandrian grain ships; St Paul landed here (Acts 28:13).

eras.name: Puteoli
eras.note: Declining harbour town; the grain fleets now unload at Portus.

eras.name: Puteoli
eras.note: A declining harbour town; trade has largely moved to Portus.

eras.name: Capua
eras.note: Rich Campanian city on the Via Appia, famed for bronze work, perfumes and gladiator schools.

eras.name: Capua
eras.note: Seat of the governor of Campania.

eras.name: Capua
eras.note: Still a junction on the Via Appia under Ostrogothic rule.

eras.name: Capua
eras.note: Narses defeated the Franks and Alamanni near here at the Casilinus in 554.

eras.name: Taras
eras.note: Spartan colony with the best harbour in southern Italy; a leading city of Magna Graecia.

eras.name: Tarentum
eras.note: A quiet Roman municipium on the Via Appia, past its Hellenistic glory.

eras.name: Tarentum
eras.note: Port town of Calabria.

eras.name: Tarentum
eras.note: Port town of Ostrogothic Italy.

eras.name: Tarentum
eras.note: Roman port in the south.

eras.name: Brundisium
eras.note: End of the Via Appia and the usual port for the crossing to Greece and the East.

eras.name: Brundisium
eras.note: Crossing port to the Balkans.

eras.name: Brundisium
eras.note: Adriatic port of Ostrogothic Italy, facing the Eastern Empire across the strait.

eras.name: Brundisium
eras.note: Adriatic port.

eras.name: Ariminum
eras.note: Where the Via Flaminia from Rome meets the Via Aemilia to the Po valley; Augustus's arch (27 BC) still stands.

eras.name: Ariminum
eras.note: Junction of the Via Flaminia and Via Aemilia.

eras.name: Ariminum
eras.note: Road junction south of Ravenna.

eras.name: Ariminum
eras.note: Besieged in the Gothic War.

eras.name: Ravenna
eras.note: Augustus based the Adriatic fleet at nearby Classis.

eras.name: Ravenna
eras.note: Base of the Adriatic fleet at Classis.

eras.name: Ravenna
eras.note: Capital of Theoderic the Great's Ostrogothic kingdom, protected by marshes and the sea; Theoderic's palace and churches are being built.

eras.name: Ravenna
eras.note: Seat of the Roman governor of Italy (Narses). San Vitale (547) shows Justinian and Theodora in mosaic.

eras.name: Aquileia
eras.note: Great trading city at the head of the Adriatic, gateway to the Danube lands and the amber trade.

eras.name: Aquileia
eras.note: One of the great cities of Italy, with an imperial mint and residence, guarding the routes to the Balkans.

eras.name: Aquileia
eras.note: Sacked by Attila in 452 and much reduced, but still the seat of a powerful bishop (later patriarch) and the start of the road into the Balkans.

eras.name: Aquileia
eras.note: Its patriarch will flee to Grado when the Lombards invade in 568.

eras.name: Mediolanum
eras.note: Prosperous city of Cisalpine Gaul.

eras.name: Mediolanum
eras.note: Residence of Maximian, Augustus of the West; in practice the capital of Italy.

eras.name: Mediolanum
eras.note: Former imperial capital (286–402) and great see of St Ambrose, now an Ostrogothic city.

eras.name: Mediolanum
eras.note: Sacked by the Goths and Burgundians in 539, its men reportedly massacred (Procopius, Wars 6.21).

eras.name: Rhegion
eras.note: Greek colony guarding the Strait of Messina, ruled from 494 BC by the tyrant Anaxilas.

eras.name: Rhegium
eras.note: Port on the Strait of Messina where St Paul's ship waited for a south wind (Acts 28:13).

eras.name: Rhegium
eras.note: Crossing to Sicily.

eras.name: Rhegium
eras.note: Crossing point to Sicily.

eras.name: Rhegium
eras.note: Crossing to Sicily.

eras.name: Syrakousai
eras.note: Rich Corinthian colony; within a generation Gelon will make it the greatest Greek city in the west.

eras.name: Syracusae
eras.note: Capital of the Roman province of Sicily.

eras.name: Syracusae
eras.note: Chief city of Sicily, famed for its catacombs.

eras.name: Syracusae
eras.note: Chief city of Ostrogothic Sicily.

eras.name: Syracusae
eras.note: Belisarius took Sicily in 535 and celebrated his consulship here.

eras.name: Akragas
eras.note: Prosperous Greek city famed for its temples; Pindar called it "the fairest city of mortals".

eras.name: Motya
eras.note: Phoenician island-town off western Sicily, Carthage's foothold on the island.

eras.name: Lilybaeum
eras.note: Port of western Sicily, closest point to Africa.

eras.name: Lilybaeum
eras.note: Port of western Sicily.

eras.name: Lilybaeum
eras.note: Given to the Vandals c. 500 as the dowry of Theoderic's sister Amalafrida when she married King Thrasamund.

eras.name: Lilybaeum
eras.note: Roman port of western Sicily.

eras.name: Karalis
eras.note: Phoenician harbour town; Carthage has been extending its control over Sardinia.

eras.name: Carales
eras.note: Main port of Sardinia, a grain supplier of Rome.

eras.name: Carales
eras.note: Main port of Sardinia.

eras.name: Carales
eras.note: Vandal-held Sardinia's chief city.

eras.name: Carales
eras.note: Roman Sardinia since 534.

eras.name: Massalia
eras.note: Founded c. 600 BC by Greeks from Phocaea; trades wine and goods up the Rhône to the Celts.

eras.name: Massilia
eras.note: Old Greek city, still a centre of learning, now within Roman Gallia Narbonensis.

eras.name: Massilia
eras.note: Old Greek port, now a provincial city.

eras.name: Massilia
eras.note: Port held by the Visigoths (Provence passes to the Ostrogoths in 508).

eras.name: Massilia
eras.note: Frankish since 536 and their main Mediterranean port, importing papyrus, oil and spices.

eras.name: Emporion
eras.note: Greek trading post ("the market") founded by Phocaeans from Massalia.

eras.name: Gadir
eras.note: Ancient Phoenician city beyond the Pillars of Heracles, with a famous temple of Melqart; gateway to the silver of Tartessos.

eras.name: Gades
eras.note: Wealthy port of Baetica whose shipowners were famous; Strabo says it had more men of equestrian rank than any city but Rome.

eras.name: Gades
eras.note: Its golden age is past; Avienus will describe the old city as largely empty.

eras.name: Gades
eras.note: Hispano-Roman port in Visigothic-claimed Baetica.

eras.name: Gades
eras.note: Small port on the edge of Byzantine Spania.

eras.name: Hispalis
eras.note: River port on the Baetis where sea-going ships loaded olive oil for Rome.

eras.name: Hispalis
eras.note: Great river port for Baetican olive oil.

eras.name: Hispalis
eras.note: Major city of the south; Isidore of Seville will be its bishop a century later.

eras.name: Hispalis
eras.note: Visigothic city of Baetica.

eras.name: Corduba
eras.note: Capital of Hispania Baetica; birthplace of the Senecas.

eras.name: Corduba
eras.note: Home of Bishop Hosius, adviser to Constantine.

eras.name: Corduba
eras.note: Largely self-governing Hispano-Roman city.

eras.name: Corduba
eras.note: In open revolt against the Visigothic kings; Leovigild will retake it in 572.

eras.name: Carthago Nova
eras.note: Founded by Hasdrubal the Carthaginian in 227 BC; Roman colony with rich silver mines.

eras.name: Carthago Nova
eras.note: Capital of Diocletian's new province of Carthaginiensis.

eras.name: Carthago Spartaria
eras.note: Port city; it will become the capital of Byzantine Spania after 552.

eras.name: Carthago Spartaria
eras.note: Capital of Byzantine Spania, held since c. 552.

eras.name: Tarraco
eras.note: Capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, where Augustus wintered in 26–25 BC.

eras.name: Tarraco
eras.note: Capital of Tarraconensis, recovering from Frankish raids of the 260s.

eras.name: Tarraco
eras.note: Visigothic since the 470s.

eras.name: Tarraco
eras.note: Visigothic port.

eras.name: Narbo Martius
eras.note: First Roman colony in Gaul (118 BC) and capital of Gallia Narbonensis, on the Via Domitia.

eras.name: Narbo
eras.note: Old provincial capital on the Via Domitia.

eras.name: Narbo
eras.note: Visigothic city.

eras.name: Narbo
eras.note: Chief city of Visigothic Septimania.

eras.name: Tolosa
eras.note: Town on the route from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

eras.name: Tolosa
eras.note: Garonne city on the route to the Atlantic.

eras.name: Tolosa
eras.note: Capital of the Visigothic kingdom of Alaric II, until his defeat by Clovis at Vouillé in 507.

eras.name: Tolosa
eras.note: Frankish since 507.

eras.name: Arelate
eras.note: Colony of Caesar's veterans and Rhône river port.

eras.name: Arelate
eras.note: Prosperous Rhône port; Constantine will favour it and the church council of 314 will meet here.

eras.name: Arelate
eras.note: Seat of the Prefecture of the Gauls since c. 407; held by the Visigoths in 500.

eras.name: Arelate
eras.note: Frankish city, whose bishop Caesarius (d. 542) was a famous preacher.

eras.name: Lugdunum
eras.note: Founded in 43 BC, capital of the Three Gauls and hub of Agrippa's road network.

eras.name: Lugdunum
eras.note: Former capital of the Three Gauls, still an important mint, though it suffered in the civil war of 197.

eras.name: Lugdunum
eras.note: A royal seat of the Burgundian kings.

eras.name: Lugdunum
eras.note: Frankish since the conquest of Burgundy in 534.

eras.name: Qart-Hadasht
eras.note: Phoenician "New City", leader of the western Phoenician world, controlling sea lanes from Sicily to the Atlantic.

eras.name: Ruins of Carthage
eras.note: Razed by Scipio Aemilianus in 146 BC; Utica is now the capital of Roman Africa. Gaius Gracchus's colony "Junonia" (122 BC) briefly settled nearby, and Caesar will refound the city in 44 BC.

eras.name: Carthago
eras.note: Destroyed in 146 BC, refounded as a Roman colony by Caesar and Augustus; capital of Africa Proconsularis.

eras.name: Carthago
eras.note: Second city of the West, capital of Africa Proconsularis and a great Christian centre (Cyprian's see).

eras.name: Carthago
eras.note: Capital of the Vandal kingdom (since 439), ruled by King Thrasamund.

eras.name: Carthago
eras.note: Capital of Roman Africa, reconquered by Belisarius in 533.

eras.name: Lepcis Magna
eras.note: Punic trading town flourishing under Rome; its theatre was dedicated in AD 1–2.

eras.name: Lepcis Magna
eras.note: Home town of Septimius Severus, magnificently rebuilt by him c. 200; capital of Diocletian's new province of Tripolitania.

eras.name: Lepcis Magna
eras.note: Declining town in the Vandal kingdom, harried by desert raiders.

eras.name: Lepcis Magna
eras.note: Reduced to a small walled core, its harbour silting up (Procopius, Buildings 6.4).

eras.name: Iol Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of the client king Juba II of Mauretania and his wife Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Antony and Cleopatra.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of Mauretania Caesariensis.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Coastal city between Vandal and Moorish rule.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Isolated Roman outpost reached by sea.

eras.name: Tingis
eras.note: Port on the African side of the Strait of Gibraltar.

eras.name: Tingis
eras.note: Capital of Mauretania Tingitana, which Diocletian attached to the Diocese of the Spains.

eras.name: Tingis
eras.note: Strait port, crossing point to Spain.

eras.name: Tingis
eras.note: Under Moorish control; the Romans hold the fortress of Septem (Ceuta) nearby.

eras.name: Kyrene
eras.note: Greek colony founded from Thera c. 631 BC, rich from horses and silphium; under Persian suzerainty.

eras.name: Cyrene
eras.note: Capital of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrenaica.

eras.name: Cyrene
eras.note: Shrinking city of Libya Superior, damaged by earthquake in 262.

eras.name: Cyrene
eras.note: A shrinking city of the Eastern Empire.

eras.name: Cyrene
eras.note: A small town; the provincial capital has moved to Ptolemais.

eras.name: Naukratis
eras.note: Greek trading port on the Canopic branch of the Nile; under Pharaoh Amasis the only Egyptian port open to Greek merchants (Herodotus 2.178–179).

eras.name: Memphis
eras.note: Ancient capital of Egypt, seat of the Persian satrap since Cambyses's conquest in 525 BC.

eras.name: Memphis
eras.note: Still a great religious centre; Strabo describes its temple of Apis.

eras.name: Memphis
eras.note: Faded ancient capital.

eras.name: Alexandria
eras.note: Second city of the empire, home of the Library and the Pharos lighthouse; Strabo calls it the greatest emporium in the world.

eras.name: Alexandria
eras.note: Diocletian besieged the city for eight months in 297–298 to crush a revolt; the column now called "Pompey's Pillar" was raised in his honour.

eras.name: Alexandria
eras.note: Great Christian city and source of Constantinople's grain.

eras.name: Alexandria
eras.note: Source of Constantinople's grain, divided between rival Christian churches.

eras.name: Pelusium
eras.note: Fortress at the eastern gate of Egypt, where Cambyses defeated the last Saite pharaoh in 525 BC.

eras.name: Pelusium
eras.note: Frontier city of Roman Egypt on the road from Syria.

eras.name: Pelusium
eras.note: Eastern gateway of Egypt.

eras.name: Pelusium
eras.note: Frontier city and stop for pilgrims to Sinai and Jerusalem.

eras.name: Pelusium
eras.note: Where the Plague of Justinian first appeared in 541 (Procopius, Wars 2.22).

eras.name: Gaza (Kadytis)
eras.note: Herodotus's "Kadytis", a city "not much smaller than Sardis", on the road from Phoenicia to Egypt.

eras.name: Gaza
eras.note: Terminus of the incense road from Arabia.

eras.name: Gaza
eras.note: Prosperous pagan city with its temple of Marnas.

eras.name: Gaza
eras.note: Flourishing centre of rhetoric and the wine trade.

eras.name: Gaza
eras.note: Famous for its wine, shipped all over the Mediterranean, and its school of rhetoric.

eras.name: Yafo (Joppa)
eras.note: Port where cedar from Lebanon was landed for the rebuilding of the Jerusalem Temple (Ezra 3:7).

eras.name: Joppa
eras.note: Old port of Judaea, overshadowed by Caesarea.

eras.name: Joppa
eras.note: Small port of Palaestina.

eras.name: Joppa
eras.note: Landing place for Holy Land pilgrims.

eras.name: Joppa
eras.note: Pilgrim port.

eras.name: Yerushalayim
eras.note: Small capital of the Persian province of Yehud; the Second Temple was completed c. 516 BC.

eras.name: Hierosolyma
eras.note: Herod the Great's rebuilt Temple is one of the wonders of the East.

eras.name: Aelia Capitolina
eras.note: Hadrian's small Roman colony on the site of Jerusalem. Christian pilgrims already come to see the holy places.

eras.name: Hierosolyma
eras.note: Christianity's holy city, full of churches and pilgrims.

eras.name: Hierosolyma
eras.note: Justinian's Nea Church (543) joins the Holy Sepulchre; the Madaba Map shows the city.

eras.name: Caesarea Maritima
eras.note: Herod's new port city (c. 22–10 BC) with a huge artificial harbour; seat of the Roman governors of Judaea.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of Palaestina, home of Origen's library; Eusebius, the church historian, works here.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of Palaestina Prima; hometown of the historian Procopius.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of Palaestina Prima, home of the historian Procopius.

eras.name: Tyre
eras.note: Island city whose merchants founded Carthage and Gadir; its fleet serves the Persian king.

eras.name: Tyrus
eras.note: Famous for purple dye and glass.

eras.name: Tyrus
eras.note: Metropolis of Phoenicia, famous for purple dye.

eras.name: Tyrus
eras.note: Metropolis of Phoenice; silk weaving and purple dyeing.

eras.name: Tyrus
eras.note: Silk-weaving city.

eras.name: Sidon
eras.note: Leading Phoenician city under Persia; its ships were the best in Xerxes's fleet.

eras.name: Sidon
eras.note: Phoenician port where St Paul visited friends (Acts 27:3).

eras.name: Sidon
eras.note: Phoenician coastal city.

eras.name: Sidon
eras.note: Coastal city on the pilgrim road.

eras.name: Sidon
eras.note: Coastal city.

eras.name: Dimashq
eras.note: Oasis city of the Persian satrapy "Beyond the River".

eras.name: Damascus
eras.note: Caravan city of the Decapolis.

eras.name: Damascus
eras.note: Arsenal city and start of the Strata Diocletiana.

eras.name: Damascus
eras.note: Strong city of the Eastern frontier.

eras.name: Damascus
eras.note: Frontier city near the Ghassanid camps.

eras.name: Raqmu (Petra)
eras.note: Rock-cut capital of the Nabataean king Aretas IV, grown rich on the incense trade.

eras.name: Petra
eras.note: Former Nabataean capital, now a city of the province of Arabia (annexed 106).

eras.name: Petra
eras.note: Still a bishopric; papyri found in its church (the Petra Papyri) record property dealings in the 6th century.

eras.name: Tadmor (Palmyra)
eras.note: Desert oasis whose caravans link the Roman world with Parthian Mesopotamia; the Temple of Bel is dedicated in AD 32.

eras.name: Palmyra
eras.note: Sacked by Aurelian in 273 after Queen Zenobia's revolt, now a garrison town with the "Camp of Diocletian" on the Strata Diocletiana.

eras.name: Antiochia
eras.note: Capital of Roman Syria and third city of the empire; its port is Seleucia Pieria.

eras.name: Antiochia
eras.note: Great city of the East and the emperors' base for the Persian wars; Diocletian built a palace here.

eras.name: Antiochia
eras.note: One of the great cities of the East, seat of a patriarch.

eras.name: Theoupolis (Antioch)
eras.note: Sacked by Khosrow I in 540, rebuilt by Justinian and renamed "City of God".

eras.name: Zeugma
eras.note: Its name means "bridge": the main Euphrates crossing between Roman Syria and Parthia.

eras.name: Edessa (Urhay)
eras.note: Capital of the small kingdom of Osrhoene under its Abgar kings, between Rome and Parthia. The Roman disaster at Carrhae (53 BC) happened nearby.

eras.name: Edessa
eras.note: Capital of Osrhoene, an early centre of Syriac Christianity.

eras.name: Edessa
eras.note: Frontier stronghold and centre of Syriac Christian learning; besieged by the Persians in 503.

eras.name: Edessa
eras.note: Proud of its image of Christ (the Mandylion), credited with saving it from Khosrow in 544.

eras.name: Nisibis
eras.note: Roman again since the Peace of Nisibis (299), and named in that treaty as the only legal crossing point for Roman–Persian trade (Peter the Patrician, fr. 14).

eras.name: Nisibis
eras.note: Persian frontier city, one of only three places where Roman–Persian trade was legally allowed (Codex Justinianus 4.63.4, AD 408/9).

eras.name: Nisibis
eras.note: Persian frontier city with a famous Christian (Church of the East) school.

eras.name: Ctesiphon
eras.note: Parthian winter capital on the Tigris, opposite the Greek city of Seleucia.

eras.name: Ctesiphon
eras.note: Capital of the Sasanian king Narseh, defeated by Galerius in 298.

eras.name: Ctesiphon
eras.note: Capital of the Sasanian king Kavad I; its great arched palace hall survives.

eras.name: Ctesiphon
eras.note: Capital of Khosrow I Anushirvan, with its great vaulted palace hall, the Taq Kasra.

eras.name: Babylon
eras.note: One of the largest cities in the world and a royal capital of the Persian kings.

eras.name: Susa
eras.note: Administrative capital of Darius I, end point of the Royal Road from Sardis.

eras.name: Tarsus
eras.note: Seat of the Cilician kings under Persia, below the Cilician Gates.

eras.name: Tarsus
eras.note: Capital of Cilicia, famous for its schools; birthplace of St Paul.

eras.name: Tarsus
eras.note: Capital of Cilicia.

eras.name: Tarsus
eras.note: Stop on the pilgrim road to Jerusalem.

eras.name: Tarsus
eras.note: Cilician city.

eras.name: Salamis
eras.note: Leading city-kingdom of Cyprus; it will join the Ionian Revolt in 499 BC.

eras.name: Salamis
eras.note: Port city of Roman Cyprus.

eras.name: Salamis
eras.note: Chief city of Cyprus.

eras.name: Constantia
eras.note: Rebuilt and renamed after earthquakes; metropolis of Cyprus.

eras.name: Constantia
eras.note: Metropolis of Cyprus.

eras.name: Sparda (Sardis)
eras.note: Former Lydian capital of Croesus, now seat of the Persian satrap and start of the Royal Road.

eras.name: Sardes
eras.note: City of Roman Asia recovering from the earthquake of AD 17.

eras.name: Sardis
eras.note: Capital of Diocletian's new province of Lydia.

eras.name: Sardis
eras.note: Provincial city with a large synagogue.

eras.name: Sardis
eras.note: Lydian city.

eras.name: Ephesos
eras.note: Ionian city of the great temple of Artemis.

eras.name: Ephesus
eras.note: Capital of the province of Asia; one of the great cities of the East.

eras.name: Ephesus
eras.note: Capital of Asia; the rebuilt temple of Artemis still stands despite the Gothic raid of 262.

eras.name: Ephesus
eras.note: Great Christian city; site of the councils of 431 and 449.

eras.name: Ephesus
eras.note: Justinian's great basilica of St John stands on the hill.

eras.name: Miletos
eras.note: Greatest Ionian city, mother of dozens of Black Sea colonies; in 499 BC Aristagoras will lead the Ionian Revolt from here.

eras.name: Miletus
eras.note: Port city whose harbours are slowly silting up; St Paul met the Ephesian elders here (Acts 20).

eras.name: Miletus
eras.note: Its harbours are silting up.

eras.name: Pergamum
eras.note: Former Attalid capital with a great library and altar.

eras.name: Pergamum
eras.note: Famous for the Asclepieion where Galen trained.

eras.name: Lindos
eras.note: The leading town of Rhodes before the city of Rhodes was founded in 408 BC; a partner in the Greek trading post at Naukratis.

eras.name: Rhodos
eras.note: Great maritime republic and school of rhetoric; the Colossus lies fallen since 226 BC.

eras.name: Rhodos
eras.note: Island port and capital of the Province of the Islands.

eras.name: Rhodos
eras.note: Port on the grain route from Egypt to Constantinople.

eras.name: Rhodos
eras.note: Island port on the grain route.

eras.name: Myra
eras.note: Lycian city whose port Andriake was a stopping place for Alexandrian grain ships (Acts 27:5–6).

eras.name: Myra
eras.note: Lycian city. Its bishop, later known as St Nicholas, is a young man now.

eras.name: Myra
eras.note: Pilgrimage town of its 4th-century bishop, St Nicholas.

eras.name: Myra
eras.note: Pilgrimage to St Nicholas.

eras.name: Byzantion
eras.note: Megarian colony on the Bosporus, under Persian control since Darius's Scythian campaign.

eras.name: Byzantium
eras.note: A modest free Greek city controlling the Bosporus tolls.

eras.name: Byzantium
eras.note: Rebuilt by Septimius Severus after he besieged it in 193–196. Constantine will refound it as Constantinople in 330.

eras.name: Constantinopolis
eras.note: The "New Rome" of Constantine, capital of Emperor Anastasius I and the largest city of the Christian world.

eras.name: Constantinopolis
eras.note: Justinian died here on 14 November 565. Hagia Sophia (537) is the largest church in the world.

eras.name: Nicomedia
eras.note: Capital of Bithynia.

eras.name: Nicomedia
eras.note: Diocletian's capital, where he is building a great palace; the edict of the Great Persecution will be posted here in 303.

eras.name: Nicomedia
eras.note: Former residence of Diocletian; first stage on the road east from Constantinople.

eras.name: Nicomedia
eras.note: Bithynian metropolis.

eras.name: Ancyra
eras.note: Capital of Galatia; its temple preserves the "Res Gestae" of Augustus.

eras.name: Ancyra
eras.note: Capital of Galatia.

eras.name: Ancyra
eras.note: Junction on the military road to the Persian frontier.

eras.name: Ancyra
eras.note: Galatian city.

eras.name: Gordion
eras.note: Old Phrygian capital of King Midas, a station on the Royal Road.

eras.name: Sinope
eras.note: Milesian colony and the best harbour of the southern Black Sea.

eras.name: Sinope
eras.note: Former capital of Mithridates VI, now a Roman colony.

eras.name: Sinope
eras.note: Black Sea port of Pontus.

eras.name: Sinope
eras.note: Black Sea port of the Eastern Empire.

eras.name: Sinope
eras.note: Black Sea port.

eras.name: Trapezous
eras.note: Colony of Sinope; Xenophon's Ten Thousand will reach the sea here in 400 BC.

eras.name: Trapezus
eras.note: Port for trade with the Caucasus and Armenia.

eras.name: Trapezus
eras.note: Port sacked by the Goths in 257, since recovered.

eras.name: Trapezus
eras.note: Port and base for Roman operations in the Caucasus.

eras.name: Trapezus
eras.note: Base for the Lazic War.

eras.name: Pantikapaion
eras.note: Milesian colony on the Cimmerian Bosporus, exporting grain and fish.

eras.name: Panticapaeum
eras.note: Capital of the Bosporan kingdom, a Roman client.

eras.name: Panticapaeum
eras.note: Capital of the Bosporan kingdom, a Roman client.

eras.name: Bosporus
eras.note: Distant Greek city on the edge of the steppe, allied to Constantinople.

eras.name: Bosporus
eras.note: Roman outpost in Crimea since c. 528.

eras.name: Olbia
eras.note: Milesian colony at the mouth of the Bug and Dnieper; Herodotus visited and describes the Scythians around it.

eras.name: Olbia
eras.note: Rebuilt after its sack by the Getae c. 50 BC; described by Dio Chrysostom.

eras.name: Athenai
eras.note: Newly democratic after the reforms of Cleisthenes (508 BC); in 498 BC it will send ships to help the Ionian Revolt.

eras.name: Athenae
eras.note: Cultural and university town of the Roman world.

eras.name: Athenae
eras.note: University city, partly ruined by the Herulian sack of 267.

eras.name: Athenae
eras.note: The Neoplatonist Academy still teaches (until 529).

eras.name: Athenae
eras.note: Justinian closed the philosophical schools in 529.

eras.name: Korinthos
eras.note: Rich trading city on the Isthmus with two harbours and the "diolkos" ship-haulway between the gulfs.

eras.name: Ruins of Corinth
eras.note: Sacked by Mummius in 146 BC. Squatters live among the ruins, which Cicero saw, but travellers still cross the Isthmus. Caesar will refound it as a colony in 44 BC.

eras.name: Corinthus
eras.note: Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, refounded by Caesar in 44 BC; capital of Achaea.

eras.name: Corinthus
eras.note: Capital of Achaea.

eras.name: Corinthus
eras.note: Provincial capital of Achaea.

eras.name: Corinthus
eras.note: Shaken by earthquakes; Justinian walled the Isthmus.

eras.name: Sparta
eras.note: The leading military power of Greece, head of the Peloponnesian League.

eras.name: Sparta
eras.note: A free city with its old customs preserved as a tourist attraction.

eras.name: Sparta
eras.note: Provincial town.

eras.name: Kerkyra
eras.note: Corinthian colony with a strong fleet, "on the route to Italy and Sicily" (Thucydides 1.36).

eras.name: Corcyra
eras.note: Island stop on the sea route between Greece and Italy.

eras.name: Corcyra
eras.note: Island port.

eras.name: Corcyra
eras.note: Island port of the Eastern Empire.

eras.name: Corcyra
eras.note: Island port.

eras.name: Epidamnos
eras.note: Colony of Corcyra and Corinth on the Illyrian coast.

eras.name: Dyrrachium
eras.note: Western terminus of the Via Egnatia; Caesar and Pompey fought here in 48 BC.

eras.name: Dyrrachium
eras.note: Capital of Epirus Nova and head of the Via Egnatia.

eras.name: Dyrrachium
eras.note: Birthplace of the reigning emperor Anastasius I.

eras.name: Dyrrachium
eras.note: Adriatic gateway of the Via Egnatia.

eras.name: Thessalonica
eras.note: Capital of Macedonia on the Via Egnatia.

eras.name: Thessalonica
eras.note: Residence of Galerius, Caesar of the East, with his new palace, rotunda and triumphal arch celebrating his Persian victory.

eras.name: Thessalonica
eras.note: Second city of the European provinces of the Eastern Empire.

eras.name: Thessalonica
eras.note: Great city of the Balkans, protected by St Demetrius.

eras.name: Gortyn
eras.note: Leading Cretan city; its great law code was inscribed in the 5th century BC.

eras.name: Gortyna
eras.note: Capital of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrene, near the harbour of Fair Havens.

eras.name: Gortyna
eras.note: Capital of Crete.

eras.name: Gortyna
eras.note: Metropolis of Crete.

eras.name: Gortyna
eras.note: Metropolis of Crete.

eras.name: Ak-Ink (Eravisci)
eras.note: Oppidum of the Celtic Eravisci on Gellért Hill above the Danube. Pannonia was conquered by Tiberius (12–9 BC) and rose in revolt in AD 6–9. The Roman fort, the legionary fortress (c. AD 89) and the provincial capital came later.

eras.name: Aquincum
eras.note: Legionary fortress and city at its height, with two amphitheatres and a hydraulic organ (Valeria).

eras.name: Aquincum (ruins)
eras.note: Capital of Pannonia Inferior in the 2nd–4th centuries (the future emperor Hadrian was governor here c. 107), with amphitheatres, baths and an aqueduct. Pannonia was given up to the Huns in the 430s, and by 500 the half-deserted city lies outside the empire, in the lands of Germanic peoples such as the Gepids.

eras.name: Aquincum (ruins)
eras.note: In Lombard Pannonia; the Lombards will leave for Italy in 568 and the Avars will take over.

eras.name: Carnuntum
eras.note: Celtic settlement on the Danube where the Amber Road from the Baltic crossed the river. Tiberius made it his base against King Maroboduus in AD 6 (Velleius 2.109). Pliny puts it about 600 miles from the amber coast.

eras.name: Carnuntum
eras.note: Great Danube fortress-city; the emperors will meet here in 308 (the Conference of Carnuntum).

eras.name: Siscia (Segestica)
eras.note: Taken by Octavian after a siege in 35 BC (Appian, Illyrica 22–24) and a base for the conquest of Pannonia; a river port on the Sava.

eras.name: Siscia
eras.note: River port with an imperial mint.

eras.name: Siscia
eras.note: Bishop's seat and river town of Ostrogothic Pannonia Savia.

eras.name: Sirmium
eras.note: Roman outpost on the Sava; it was besieged by the rebel Breuci in AD 6 (Cassius Dio 55.29).

eras.name: Sirmium
eras.note: Imperial residence on the Sava, birthplace of the emperors Probus and Maximian.

eras.name: Sirmium
eras.note: A Tetrarchic capital and birthplace of several emperors. In 500 it is held by the Gepids; Theoderic's Goths will take it in 504.

eras.name: Sirmium
eras.note: Capital of the Gepids; it will pass to Rome in 567 and fall to the Avars in 582.

eras.name: Singidunum
eras.note: Legionary fortress of the Fourth Flavia on the Danube.

eras.name: Singidunum
eras.note: Danube fortress city of the Eastern Empire, founded as a Celtic (Scordiscan) settlement.

eras.name: Singidunum
eras.note: Roman Danube fortress rebuilt by Justinian.

eras.name: Naissus
eras.note: Birthplace of Constantine (c. 272).

eras.name: Naissus
eras.note: Birthplace of Constantine the Great. Sacked by Attila in 441: in 448 the envoy Priscus found it deserted, with the riverbank full of bones.

eras.name: Naissus
eras.note: Rebuilt by Justinian.

eras.name: Serdica
eras.note: Capital of Dacia Mediterranea; Galerius will die here in 311.

eras.name: Serdica
eras.note: Constantine is said to have called it "my Rome". It hosted the church council of 343 and is a major stop on the Via Militaris.

eras.name: Serdica
eras.note: Strong city on the Via Militaris.

eras.name: Salona
eras.note: Colonia Martia Iulia Salona, capital of Illyricum (later Dalmatia), a port and the base for the conquest of the interior.

eras.name: Salona
eras.note: Capital of Dalmatia and home town of Diocletian.

eras.name: Salona
eras.note: Great Christian metropolis of Dalmatia, ruled by Theoderic since 493. Diocletian was born nearby.

eras.name: Salona
eras.note: Roman again since 535; it will be destroyed by Avars and Slavs c. 614.

eras.name: Diocletian's Palace (building)
eras.note: The emperor's retirement palace is under construction on the bay of Aspalathos; he will move in after abdicating in 305.

eras.name: Diocletian's Palace (Spalatum)
eras.note: The vast fortified retirement palace that Diocletian built c. 295–305 and lived in after his abdication in 305. Asked to return to power, he said he would rather show off the cabbages he grew at Salona (Epitome de Caesaribus 39.6). The last western emperor, Julius Nepos, was murdered at his villa near Salona in 480.

eras.name: Diocletian's Palace (Spalatum)
eras.note: Still standing; refugees from Salona will settle inside its walls in the 7th century, founding the city of Split.

eras.name: Delphoi
eras.note: The oracle of Apollo, the "navel of the world". Kings like Croesus consulted it (Herodotus 1.46–55), and the Athenian Alcmaeonid family has just rebuilt its temple after the fire of 548 BC.

eras.name: Delphi
eras.note: The oracle is still consulted but in decline. Its treasuries are full of statues, many carried off by Roman generals.

eras.name: Delphi
eras.note: The oracle still functions, but in decline.

eras.name: Delphi
eras.note: The oracle fell silent in the late 4th century; Delphi is now a small Christian town with a basilica among the ruined treasuries.

eras.name: Olympia
eras.note: Sanctuary of Zeus where the Olympic Games have been held every four years since, by tradition, 776 BC.

eras.name: Olympia
eras.note: Home of Phidias's gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders. The games continue; Nero will compete in AD 67.

eras.name: Olympia
eras.note: The games continue; the last known victor is recorded in 385.

eras.name: Delos
eras.note: Sacred island where Apollo and Artemis were born. Peisistratus purified it (Herodotus 1.64) and Polycrates of Samos dedicated neighbouring Rheneia to Apollo (Thucydides 3.104).

eras.name: Nicopolis
eras.note: "Victory City", founded by Octavian beside the battlefield of Actium (31 BC), where he defeated Antony and Cleopatra (Strabo 7.7.6).

eras.name: Nicopolis
eras.note: Capital of Epirus Vetus.

eras.name: Nicopolis
eras.note: Capital of the province of Epirus Vetus.

eras.name: Nicopolis
eras.note: Shrinking capital of Epirus.

eras.name: Samos
eras.note: Polycrates' island city (he died c. 522). Herodotus (3.60) singles out its three greatest works of engineering: the tunnel of Eupalinos, the harbour mole and the temple of Hera.

eras.name: Paphos
eras.note: Kingdom famous for its sanctuary of Aphrodite, who came ashore here after her birth from the sea (Odyssey 8.362–363; Herodotus 1.105).

eras.name: Paphos
eras.note: Seat of the Roman governor of Cyprus. Paul met the proconsul Sergius Paulus here (Acts 13:6–12).

eras.name: Halikarnassos
eras.note: Dorian city ruled by a Carian dynasty under Persia. Its queen Artemisia will command ships at Salamis in 480 (Herodotus 7.99), and Herodotus himself is born here c. 484 BC.

eras.name: Halicarnassus
eras.note: Home of the Mausoleum (c. 350 BC), the tomb of Mausolus and one of the Seven Wonders.

eras.name: Halicarnassus
eras.note: The Mausoleum still stands.

eras.name: Halicarnassus
eras.note: The Mausoleum still stands. It is thought to have fallen in medieval earthquakes, and the Knights of St John later quarried it.

eras.name: Halicarnassus
eras.note: The Mausoleum still stands.

eras.name: Didyma (Branchidai)
eras.note: Oracle of Apollo run by the Branchidae, enriched by Croesus (Herodotus 1.46, 1.92). The Persians will sack it after the Ionian Revolt (Herodotus 6.19).

eras.name: Didyma
eras.note: The colossal Hellenistic temple of Apollo is still under construction; it was never finished.

eras.name: Ilion
eras.note: Small Aeolian town on the site of Homer's Troy. Xerxes will sacrifice a thousand oxen to Athena of Ilion in 480 (Herodotus 7.43).

eras.name: Ilium
eras.note: Favoured by Caesar and Augustus as the ancestral home of the Julii, descendants of Aeneas (Strabo 13.1.27).

eras.name: Hierapolis
eras.note: Spa town on the white travertine terraces. Strabo (13.4.14) tested its deadly "Plutonium" cave by releasing sparrows into it.

eras.name: Hierapolis
eras.note: Spa town with its Plutonium and theatre.

eras.name: Hierapolis
eras.note: Pilgrimage centre with the martyrium of the apostle Philip (early 5th century).

eras.name: Hierapolis
eras.note: Pilgrimage to St Philip.

eras.name: Mazaca / Caesarea
eras.note: Capital of King Archelaus of Cappadocia, renamed Caesarea in honour of Augustus, below Mount Argaeus (Strabo 12.2.7–9).

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Metropolis of Cappadocia.

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Metropolis of Cappadocia, see of St Basil the Great (d. 379).

eras.name: Caesarea
eras.note: Cappadocian metropolis.

eras.name: Tomis
eras.note: Greek trading colony on the western Black Sea coast.

eras.name: Tomis
eras.note: Augustus exiled the poet Ovid here in AD 8; his Tristia and Letters from Pontus complain of the cold, the Getae and the frozen sea.

eras.name: Tomis
eras.note: Capital of Scythia Minor.

eras.name: Tomis
eras.note: Capital of the frontier province of Scythia Minor.

eras.name: Tomis
eras.note: Frontier city facing the newly arrived Avars.

eras.name: Phasis
eras.note: Milesian colony in Colchis, the land of the Golden Fleece sought by the Argonauts.

eras.name: Phasis
eras.note: Port at the eastern end of the Black Sea (Strabo 11.2.17).

eras.name: Phasis
eras.note: Roman fort in Colchis.

eras.name: Phasis
eras.note: Port of Lazica, a Roman ally; Rome and Persia will fight over it in the Lazic War (541–562).

eras.name: Phasis
eras.note: Port of Lazica, fought over until the Fifty-Year Peace of 562.

eras.name: Tanais
eras.note: Bosporan emporium at the mouth of the Don, where steppe nomads traded slaves and hides for wine and cloth (Strabo 11.2.3).

eras.name: Chersonesus
eras.note: Dorian Greek city (founded 422/1 BC) in the south-west of Crimea, under Bosporan and Roman protection.

eras.name: Chersonesus
eras.note: Greek city of Crimea under Roman protection.

eras.name: Cherson
eras.note: The Eastern Empire's outpost in Crimea and a place of exile.

eras.name: Cherson
eras.note: Roman city of Crimea.

eras.name: Artaxata
eras.note: Capital of Armenia, said to have been laid out on Hannibal's advice (Strabo 11.14.6; Plutarch, Lucullus 31). Rome and Parthia compete for control of Armenia.

eras.name: Artaxata
eras.note: Capital of King Tiridates III of Armenia, restored with Roman help; Armenia will become the first Christian kingdom c. 301.

eras.name: Artaxata / Dvin
eras.note: In Persian Armenia; one of only three places where Roman–Persian trade was legally allowed (Codex Justinianus 4.63.4).

eras.name: Dvin
eras.note: Capital of Persian Armenia.

eras.name: Hierothesion of Antiochus I (Nemrud Dağ)
eras.note: Mountain-top tomb sanctuary of King Antiochus I of Commagene (r. c. 70–38 BC), with colossal statues of the king beside Greek and Persian gods. Commagene stays a client kingdom until AD 17 (Tacitus, Annals 2.42).

eras.name: Pyramids of Khufu
eras.note: Already over 2,000 years old. Herodotus heard that 100,000 men worked for twenty years to build the Great Pyramid (2.124–127).

eras.name: The Pyramids
eras.note: A must-see for Roman tourists. Strabo (17.1.33) and Pliny (36.75–82) describe them.

eras.name: The Pyramids
eras.note: Visited by Roman tourists, who scratched graffiti on them.

eras.name: The Pyramids
eras.note: Still clad in their white limestone casing; Christian travellers sometimes call them "Joseph's granaries".

eras.name: The Pyramids
eras.note: Still clad in their casing stones.

eras.name: Babylon (Egypt)
eras.note: Fortress at the head of the Delta, garrisoned by one of Egypt's three Roman legions (Strabo 17.1.30).

eras.name: Babylon (Egypt)
eras.note: Fortress at the apex of the Delta, rebuilt as a strong fort around this time.

eras.name: Babylon (Egypt)
eras.note: Roman fortress city at the apex of the Delta, the site of later Cairo.

eras.name: Babylon (Egypt)
eras.note: Fortress city at the apex of the Delta; it will fall to the Arabs in 641.

eras.name: Waset (Thebes)
eras.note: Homer's "hundred-gated Thebes", with the vast temples of Karnak and Luxor.

eras.name: Thebes (Diospolis)
eras.note: Tourists visit the Valley of the Kings and the "singing" Colossus of Memnon. Strabo heard its sound at dawn but suspected a trick (17.1.46).

eras.name: Thebes (Luxor)
eras.note: The Luxor temple has been converted into a legionary fortress, with an imperial-cult chamber painted with the Tetrarchs.

eras.name: Thebes
eras.note: Monks and hermits live among the old tombs and temples.

eras.name: Thebes
eras.note: Monasteries and the village of Djeme fill the old temples.

eras.name: Swenet / Elephantine
eras.note: Frontier at the First Cataract. Persian-era papyri record a Jewish military colony on Elephantine island.

eras.name: Syene
eras.note: Frontier garrison. Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference from the fact that the sun shines straight down a well here at midsummer (Strabo 17.1.48; Cleomedes 1.7).

eras.name: Syene & Philae
eras.note: In 298 Diocletian pulled the frontier back to here and Philae, paying the Nobatae and Blemmyes to guard the south (Procopius, Wars 1.19).

eras.name: Syene
eras.note: Southern frontier. Nearby Philae is the last working temple of Isis; Justinian will close it c. 535 (Procopius, Wars 1.19).

eras.name: Syene
eras.note: Justinian closed the temple of Isis at Philae c. 537 (Procopius, Wars 1.19).

eras.name: Meroë
eras.note: Herodotus heard of Meroë as "the mother-city of the Ethiopians" (2.29). Cambyses' expedition against the Ethiopians failed (3.25).

eras.name: Meroë
eras.note: Royal city of the Kingdom of Kush, with its pyramids. Its queen (the "Kandake") fought Rome in 24–22 BC (Strabo 17.1.54); a bronze head of Augustus looted then was buried here.

eras.name: Meroë
eras.note: The Kingdom of Kush is in decline; Aksumite armies will sack the region c. 350.

eras.name: Myos Hormos
eras.note: Red Sea port for the India trade. Strabo saw up to 120 ships a year sailing from here to India (2.5.12; Periplus Maris Erythraei 1).

eras.name: Oracle of Ammon
eras.note: Desert oracle consulted even by Croesus (Herodotus 1.46). An army Cambyses sent against it vanished in a sandstorm (3.26).

eras.name: Ammonium
eras.note: Alexander was greeted here as son of Zeus-Ammon in 331 BC, but Strabo says the oracle is now almost abandoned (17.1.43).

eras.name: Garama (Garamantes)
eras.note: Capital of the Garamantes, who according to Herodotus hunted "cave-dwelling Ethiopians" in four-horse chariots (4.183).

eras.name: Garama
eras.note: Saharan kingdom controlling caravan routes; Cornelius Balbus celebrated a triumph over the Garamantes in 19 BC (Pliny 5.35–38).

eras.name: Garama
eras.note: Capital of the Saharan Garamantes, trading with Roman Tripolitania.

eras.name: Garama
eras.note: The Garamantian kingdom survives; it will make peace with Constantinople and accept Christianity c. 569.

eras.name: Garama
eras.note: The Garamantes will make peace with Rome and accept Christianity c. 569.

eras.name: Shrine of St Menas
eras.note: Great pilgrimage centre in the desert west of Alexandria, enlarged by Emperor Zeno. Pilgrims took home clay flasks ("Menas ampullae") of holy water, which have been found as far away as Britain.

eras.name: Shrine of St Menas
eras.note: At its height: a pilgrim city with a great basilica and baths.

eras.name: Mount Sinai
eras.note: Hermits and a church of the Burning Bush. The pilgrim Egeria climbed the mountain in 383; Justinian will fortify the monastery c. 550.

eras.name: Monastery of Mount Sinai
eras.note: Justinian has built the fortified monastery at the Burning Bush, later St Catherine's.

eras.name: Berytus
eras.note: Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Berytus, settled with veterans by Agrippa in 15/14 BC (Strabo 16.2.19).

eras.name: Berytus
eras.note: Seat of the empire's leading law school.

eras.name: Berytus
eras.note: Famous for its law school, the best in the East, until the earthquake of 551.

eras.name: Berytus
eras.note: Ruined by the earthquake and tsunami of 551; its law school moved to Sidon.

eras.name: Heliopolis (Baalbek)
eras.note: Roman colony where the colossal temple of Jupiter Heliopolitanus is being built on enormous stone blocks.

eras.name: Heliopolis
eras.note: The temple complex of Jupiter, Venus and Bacchus is complete and still busy with pilgrims.

eras.name: Heliopolis
eras.note: The giant temples still dominate the town; a Christian basilica now stands in the sanctuary court.

eras.name: Heliopolis
eras.note: Its giant temples are partly ruined.

eras.name: Masada
eras.note: Herod's fortress-palace on a desert mesa above the Dead Sea, with hanging terraces and huge cisterns (Josephus, Jewish War 7.280–303). The rebels' last stand against Rome will come in AD 73–74.

eras.name: Bethlehem
eras.note: Small Judaean town, the city of David and, in the Gospels, the birthplace of Jesus (Matthew 2; Luke 2).

eras.name: Bethlehem
eras.note: Village where Christians already show visitors the cave of the Nativity (Origen, Against Celsus 1.51).

eras.name: Bethlehem
eras.note: Pilgrims visit Constantine's Church of the Nativity; Jerome translated the Bible here (386–420).

eras.name: Bethlehem
eras.note: Justinian has rebuilt the Church of the Nativity.

eras.name: Shrine of St Simeon Stylites
eras.note: A huge cross-shaped church (c. 476–490) built around the pillar on which Simeon lived for decades (died 459). Pilgrims flocked here (Theodoret, Religious History 26).

eras.name: Shrine of St Simeon Stylites
eras.note: Major pilgrimage centre.

eras.name: Rosafa
eras.note: Desert fort on the Strata Diocletiana. The soldier Sergius will be martyred here c. 303, and his shrine will make it a great pilgrimage city.

eras.name: Sergiopolis (Resafa)
eras.note: Desert pilgrimage city of the martyr St Sergius, revered by Romans and Arab tribes alike (Procopius, Buildings 2.9).

eras.name: Sergiopolis
eras.note: Pilgrimage city of St Sergius with new walls and cisterns.

eras.name: Charax Spasinou
eras.note: Capital of Characene at the head of the Gulf, a port for the India trade and home town of the geographer Isidore of Charax (Pliny 6.138–140).

eras.name: Hagmatana (Ecbatana)
eras.note: Old Median capital and summer residence of the Persian kings; Herodotus describes seven circuits of walls, each a different colour (1.98).

eras.name: Ecbatana
eras.note: Summer residence of the Parthian kings, who wintered at Ctesiphon (Strabo 16.1.16).

eras.name: Hamadan
eras.note: Sasanian city on the Khorasan road.

eras.name: Hamadan
eras.note: Sasanian city on the great Khorasan road.

eras.name: Hamadan
eras.note: Sasanian city.

eras.name: Behistun Rock
eras.note: Darius I has just carved his huge inscription and relief (c. 520 BC) high on the cliff, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. It later became the key to deciphering cuneiform.

eras.name: Bagistana
eras.note: Station on the road from Mesopotamia into Iran. Greek writers credited the relief to Queen Semiramis (Diodorus 2.13; Isidore of Charax 5).

eras.name: Bisotun
eras.note: Station on the royal road; Darius's relief looks down on passing caravans.

eras.name: Bisotun
eras.note: Stage on the Sasanian royal road near Kermanshah, a district of Sasanian rock reliefs.

eras.name: Bisotun
eras.note: Royal road station with an unfinished Sasanian building programme.

eras.name: Parsa (Persepolis)
eras.note: Darius's ceremonial capital, under construction since c. 518 BC. Thousands of clay tablets from its archive record rations for workers and travellers on the royal roads.

eras.name: Utica
eras.note: Phoenician colony said to be older than Carthage (Velleius 1.2; Pliny 16.216).

eras.name: Utica
eras.note: Capital of Roman Africa after 146 BC. Cato the Younger killed himself here in 46 BC rather than surrender to Caesar (Plutarch, Cato Minor 70).

eras.name: Utica
eras.note: Old provincial capital, its harbour silting up.

eras.name: Hippo Regius
eras.note: Port that was once a residence of the Numidian kings (hence "Regius").

eras.name: Hippo Regius
eras.note: Busy port of Numidia.

eras.name: Hippo Regius
eras.note: Augustine was its bishop from 396 and died here in 430 while the Vandals besieged the city.

eras.name: Hippo Regius
eras.note: Roman again; Augustine's library survived the Vandals.

eras.name: Volubilis
eras.note: Berber-Punic town in the realm of Juba II of Mauretania, rich from olive oil.

eras.name: Volubilis
eras.note: Abandoned by the Roman administration c. 285 when the frontier pulled back north, but still inhabited.

eras.name: Volubilis
eras.note: Outside imperial control since the late 3rd century, yet still inhabited by Latin-speaking Christians.

eras.name: Volubilis
eras.note: Christian Berber town; its last Latin inscriptions date to the 650s.

eras.name: Emerita Augusta
eras.note: Founded in 25 BC for veterans of the Cantabrian wars; capital of Lusitania, with a new theatre given by Agrippa.

eras.name: Emerita Augusta
eras.note: Seat of the vicar of the new Diocese of the Spains.

eras.name: Emerita
eras.note: Seat of the Diocese of the Spains and the shrine of St Eulalia (Prudentius, Peristephanon 3).

eras.name: Emerita
eras.note: Rich Visigothic city with famous bishops (Lives of the Fathers of Mérida).

eras.name: Olisipo
eras.note: Felicitas Julia Olisipo on the Tagus estuary, the Atlantic edge of the empire. Pliny repeats the tale that local mares conceived by the west wind (8.166).

eras.name: Olisipo
eras.note: Atlantic port of Lusitania.

eras.name: Olisipo
eras.note: Contested between the Sueves and the Visigoths.

eras.name: Olisipo
eras.note: Visigothic town on the Tagus.

eras.name: Burdigala
eras.note: Emporium of the Bituriges Vivisci on the Garonne estuary (Strabo 4.2.1).

eras.name: Burdigala
eras.note: Wealthy port and wine town of Aquitania; the poet Ausonius is born here c. 310.

eras.name: Burdigala
eras.note: Home of the poet Ausonius, and the starting point of the Bordeaux Pilgrim's journey to Jerusalem in 333. Now Visigothic.

eras.name: Burdigala
eras.note: Frankish city of Aquitaine.

eras.name: Nemausus
eras.note: Augustus has given it walls; the Maison Carrée temple, dedicated to his grandsons Gaius and Lucius, is brand new.

eras.name: Nemausus
eras.note: City of Narbonensis with its amphitheatre and aqueduct.

eras.name: Nemausus
eras.note: Visigothic city. Its aqueduct, carried over the Gardon on the Pont du Gard (mid-1st century AD), no longer supplies the city.

eras.name: Nemausus
eras.note: Visigothic town of Septimania.

eras.name: Augusta Treverorum
eras.note: New town of the Treveri (founded c. 16 BC), on Agrippa's road to the Rhine.

eras.name: Augusta Treverorum
eras.note: Residence of Constantius Chlorus, Caesar of the West, with a new palace, basilica and baths; it guards the Rhine frontier.

eras.name: Treveri
eras.note: Former imperial residence of Constantine, with the Porta Nigra and the great basilica, now under Frankish rule.

eras.name: Treveri
eras.note: City of the Austrasian Frankish kingdom of Sigibert I.

eras.name: Oppidum Ubiorum
eras.note: Town of the Ubii on the Rhine with the Altar of Augustus (Ara Ubiorum), a base for campaigns into Germania.

eras.name: Colonia Agrippina
eras.note: Fortified Rhine city facing the Franks.

eras.name: Colonia Agrippina
eras.note: Seat of the Rhineland Frankish kings.

eras.name: Colonia
eras.note: Austrasian Frankish city on the Rhine.

eras.name: Lutetia
eras.note: Island town of the Parisii in the Seine (Caesar, Gallic War 6.3, 7.57; Strabo 4.3.5).

eras.name: Lutetia (Parisii)
eras.note: Walled island city on the Seine.

eras.name: Parisius
eras.note: City of St Geneviève. Clovis will make it his capital c. 508.

eras.name: Parisius
eras.note: Capital of King Charibert I (561–567).

eras.name: Turonum (Tours)
eras.note: Shrine of St Martin (d. 397), the most popular pilgrimage in Gaul, on the frontier between Franks and Visigoths. Clovis will come here after his victory in 507 (Gregory of Tours 2.37–38).

eras.name: Turonum (Tours)
eras.note: Shrine of St Martin. Gregory, the historian of the Franks, will become bishop in 573.

eras.name: Veii
eras.note: Powerful Etruscan city only 15 km from Rome, its great rival; its sculptor Vulca made the terracotta Apollo of Veii. Rome will capture it in 396 BC (Livy 5.21).

eras.name: Poseidonia
eras.note: Greek colony founded from Sybaris, with the Doric temples of Hera (c. 550 BC) and Athena (c. 500 BC).

eras.name: Paestum
eras.note: Roman colony famous for roses that bloomed twice a year (Virgil, Georgics 4.119).

eras.name: Pompeii
eras.note: Prosperous Roman colony on the Bay of Naples, buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 (Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16, 6.20).

eras.name: Londinium
eras.note: Largest city of Britain. Constantius Chlorus recovered it from the usurper Allectus in 296, as shown on the Arras medallion.

eras.name: Eboracum
eras.note: Fortress of the Sixth Legion. Constantius will die here in 306 and his son Constantine will be proclaimed emperor by the troops.

eras.name: Hadrian's Wall (Vercovicium)
eras.note: The 73-mile wall built from AD 122, still garrisoned against the Picts. Constantius campaigned beyond it in 305.

eras.name: Gesoriacum / Bononia
eras.note: Base of the British fleet (Classis Britannica); Constantius besieged and took it from the usurper Carausius in 293.

eras.name: Toletum
eras.note: Royal seat of the Visigothic king Athanagild (d. 567). It will be the kingdom's capital until 711.

eras.name: Dara (Anastasiopolis)
eras.note: Frontier fortress built by Anastasius (505–507) in sight of Persian Nisibis. Belisarius won a famous battle here in 530.

eras.name: Pachoras (Faras)
eras.note: Capital of Nobadia. Its king was converted by a mission sent by Empress Theodora in 543 (John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History 4.6–8).
